title: 26. Linux Troubleshooting Methodology
content:
# 26. Linux Troubleshooting Methodology

Troubleshooting is a disciplined loop: define the symptom, gather evidence, form a hypothesis, make one controlled change, and verify. Random commands can make incidents longer.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- turn vague reports into testable symptoms;
- collect a baseline without causing more damage;
- separate application, host, network, storage, and dependency failures;
- make small reversible changes;
- document evidence and follow-up work.

## Start with the symptom

Good incident notes begin with specifics:

```text
Who is affected?
What operation fails?
When did it start?
Is it constant or intermittent?
What changed recently?
How can we reproduce or observe it?
```

Avoid beginning with a fix. Begin with what is known.

## Baseline commands

```bash
date
hostname
uptime
free -h
df -h
df -i
systemctl --failed
ss -s
```

These commands give quick context about time, host identity, load, memory, disk, failed units, and socket state.

## Follow the request path

For an HTTP service, check layers in order:

```bash
curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
ss -lntup
journalctl -u api.service --since "30 minutes ago"
ip route
resolvectl status 2>/dev/null || cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

Local health passing but user traffic failing points toward proxy, firewall, DNS, routing, TLS, or load balancer layers.

## Resource pressure

High CPU, memory pressure, full disk, and inode exhaustion can all appear as application bugs:

```bash
top
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
free -h
dmesg -T | tail -n 50
df -h
```

Look for OOM kills, blocked I/O, runaway processes, and rapidly growing files.

## Logs and time windows

Use focused windows:

```bash
journalctl --since "1 hour ago" -p warning..alert
journalctl -u api.service --since "15 minutes ago"
```

Correlate logs with the reported start time. Time zone confusion is a common source of false leads.

## Hypothesis discipline

Before changing something, write the hypothesis:

```text
Hypothesis: api.service is failing because /var is full.
Evidence: df shows /var at 100%, logs contain ENOSPC.
Change: remove expired cache files owned by the app.
Verification: health check passes and new writes succeed.
```

This keeps action tied to evidence.

## Rollback and blast radius

Prefer reversible changes. Know how to undo a config edit, restart, package change, firewall update, or permissions change before applying it. Avoid bundling cleanup, upgrades, and tuning into one incident change.

## Practice

Given a failing local service, produce an incident timeline with symptom, baseline, evidence, hypothesis, action, verification, and prevention. Include at least one rejected hypothesis and why the evidence did not support it.
